title: Eco-Disasters 101: The Salton Sea
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Salton Sea in Southern California: how a cyclical ancient lake system (Lake Cahuilla and earlier inland seas) and a 1905-1907 Colorado River breach created a modern lake in the Salton Basin; how agricultural runoff, salinity, and eutrophication led to mass fish and bird die-offs; the resort-era boom and bust; the QSA water transfer and restoration efforts; health and dust concerns; lithium and geothermal plans; and local legends and oddities. Ends with listener mail about the MTV cut.

segments.title: Opening banter and sea vs. lake question
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Salton Sea topic, joke about its name and a 2002 movie, and debate whether it is a sea or a lake.

segments.title: Ancient inland seas and cycle of Lake Cahuilla
segments.summary: The Salton Basin is a geological trough that repeatedly filled with water from the Colorado River over tens of thousands of years, forming lakes that later dried up. Lake Cahuilla, formed about 1,300 years ago, was about 26 times the size of the modern Salton Sea. Silt built a natural dam, causing cyclical filling and drying.

segments.title: Size comparisons and Imperial Canal
segments.summary: Lake Cahuilla size is compared to places around the world. Silt made the soil fertile but the area dry, so the Imperial Canal was built in the early 1900s to divert Colorado River water for irrigation; silt soon clogged it.

segments.title: 1905 canal breach and Colorado River diversion
segments.summary: A clog led to a temporary bypass without proper headgates. A rainy season and snowmelt made the Colorado River overwhelm the bypass and flow into the basin, with about 90,000 cubic feet per second entering. Efforts to redirect it failed, and the breach was sealed in 1907 by railroad crews using rock, gravel, and clay.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a short promotional segment.

segments.title: Agricultural runoff stabilizes lake; salinity; wildlife refuge
segments.summary: Agricultural runoff from the 1920s kept the lake filled but added salt, making it saltier than the Pacific. The lake sits on the Pacific Flyway, and fish like tilapia and sportfish were stocked, leading to a wildlife refuge established by the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Flamingos and sea lions were introduced; a restaurant operated on Mullet Island, a dormant volcano.

segments.title: Salton Riviera resort era
segments.summary: In the 1950s developers marketed the area as the California Riviera or Palm Springs by the Sea, with resorts, tiki bars, celebrity performances, speedboat races, vacation homes, and the North Shore Beach and Yacht Club. Bombay Beach was a party town, but environmental problems grew through the 1970s.
topics: North Shore Beach and Yacht Club

segments.title: Eutrophication, algae blooms, and fish die-offs
segments.summary: Fertilizer and pesticide runoff caused algae and bacteria blooms, oxygen depletion, dead zones, and toxins. Massive bird die-offs followed, including 150,000 eared grebes over five months in 1991-92 and endangered brown pelicans in 1996. In 1999, about 8 million tilapia died in one day, with warm, saline water reducing oxygen as an added cause.

segments.title: Tilapia die-off and fish taco aside
segments.summary: The hosts discuss counting tilapia carcasses, the 1999 die-off record, and the previous 500,000-fish record. Incinerators ran due to smell, and the lake is shrinking, losing about 10 percent with projections of 40 percent by 2030.

segments.title: Shrinking lake, abandoned resort decline, and drive-in movie
segments.summary: Houses built on the shoreline are now far from the water. The North Shore Beach and Yacht Club closed in 1984 after a flood from runoff. A photo of a derelict drive-in theater in Bombay Beach with abandoned cars is discussed, along with a YouTube video of the site.
topics: North Shore Beach and Yacht Club closure

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short mid-episode break.

segments.title: Sulfur smell, restoration attempts, and the QSA
segments.summary: A sulfur dioxide cloud smelling of rotten eggs reached Los Angeles and was traced to the lake. Restoration to former glory was judged unfeasible. In 2003 Southern California water districts signed the Quantification Settlement Agreement, trading irrigation efficiency upgrades for Colorado River water, which reduced runoff into the sea.

segments.title: Fallow land water transfer and bird habitat
segments.summary: As part of the agreement, farmers were paid to leave land fallow to send water to the sea for fifteen years, which turned out to help. The lake remains a migratory stop on the Pacific Flyway, an important habitat as other habitats were lost to development.

segments.title: Health impacts: dust, asthma, and children's study
segments.summary: Exposed lakebed dust contains metals, pesticides, and DDT and causes problems. Researchers led by Dr. Jill Johnson at USC are following elementary school children in the Imperial Valley, finding high asthma rates; the study was published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. A 2014 Pacific Institute study estimated financial costs up to $70 billion over 30 years.
topics: Salton Sea in Children's Health study

segments.title: Restoration funding history and politics
segments.summary: Governor Gray Davis's 2003 restoration act and fund received no funding. The Army Corps of Engineers was authorized for $30 million in 2007; funding in 2015 went to a roughly $200,000 study. A ten-year plan estimated at $383 million was proposed for wetland restoration.

segments.title: Recent state and federal funding and wetland restoration; lithium and geothermal
segments.summary: California and the federal government provided roughly $200 million and $240 million under Governor Gavin Newsom, nearly half a billion total. About 2,000 acres of wetlands were restored since 2016, with plans for about 9,000 more. Geothermal plants and lithium mining near Mullet Island are being pursued, and the hosts discuss the tradeoffs.

segments.title: Urban legends, Navy bombs, lost ship, and local art
segments.summary: The Navy used the lake for bombing practice, including possibly practicing atomic bomb drops, and locals believe an atomic bomb is hidden there; about 24 sunken planes are in the sea. The Lost Ship of the Desert legend is discussed. Bombay Beach's dive bar sits below sea level, and the area has art sites like Salvation Mountain, East Jesus, and Slab City.

segments.title: Wrap-up and plug for Ben Hackett's album
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the Salton Sea topic and plug producer Ben Hackett's record Songs for Sleeping Dogs.

segments.title: Listener mail on the MTV cut
segments.summary: A listener from Chris Singleton, an ops manager at Independence Rock Media, writes about the MTV cut, noting average shot length fell from about eight seconds to two seconds. The hosts discuss whether viewing habits changed and how to send email.
